Led by Frank Keutsch and his team, the initiative was presented at the American Geophysical Union Fall Meeting in 2017. Importantly, this experiment was not an attempt to deploy geoengineering techniques for cooling the planet but rather a scientific endeavor to refine computer models assessing the implications of solar geoengineering, particularly regarding stratospheric heating and its potential impacts on ecosystems.

As of March 2024, Keutsch indicated that SCoPEx would no longer move forward, and the platform is likely to be redirected towards unrelated stratospheric research.

The experiment was designed to improve computer models used to estimate risks and benefits of solar geoengineering (solar radiation management). A 2021 platform test in Sweden, planned with the Swedish Space Corporation from Esrange, was a hardware test only: the SCoPEx Advisory Committee recommended suspending it pending societal engagement, and no particles were to be released. In March 2024 Harvard announced that Keutsch was no longer pursuing SCoPEx; the platform is expected to be repurposed for stratospheric research unrelated to solar geoengineering.

It is crucial to assess polar bear populations as distinct management units due to their variability. Additional stressors, including conservation hunting quotas and pollution, exacerbate the effects of declining sea ice, highlighting that claims of polar bears thriving due to chemtrails or dismissing global warming based on selective subpopulation observations lack scientific support.
